newsitem.title: USA: Heaving not a major issue yet for U.S. SRW wheat.
newsitem.headline: Heaving not a major issue yet for U.S. SRW wheat.

text.p: Concern that recent temperature swings in key U.S. soft red winter wheat growing areas may have caused heaving and hurt fledgling crops appears to be largely unfounded, agronomists said Tuesday.
"We have had some of the right kind of weather for heaving but not enough of it to be a problem right now," said James Beuerlein, professor of agronomy at Ohio State University.
He noted the main problem in Ohio was lack of fall growth. Wet conditions delayed plantings and cooler than normal temperatures slowed early growth.
"The crop is normal to poor," he said.
Heaving, caused by intermittent freezing and thawing, pushes the wheat plant and its roots out of the ground.
Ellsworth Christmas, extension agronomist at Purdue University, said Indiana's SRW wheat crop also appeared to have escaped unscathed.
"We feel, as of today, the crop is in pretty good shape," Christmas said, noting the crop had gone into the winter in much better condition than the preceding two years.
"1996 fall growth was what I would like to see. Most plants had two to four tillers in the fall, which would normally indicate a pretty good root system," he said.
Most of Indiana also had protective snow cover during the temperature swings and crops remained dormant, he said.
Christmas said his main concern had been southeast Indiana, which had little snow cover, but checks by colleagues in that area had indicated there were very few dead plants.

In Illinois snow had provided adequate cover for the winter wheat crops, according to the state's Agricultural Statistics Service. The crop was rated 10 percent excellent, 53 percent good, 33 percent fair and four percent poor, as of February 3.
Agronomists noted, however, that soft red winter wheat output was likely to be adversely affected by a drop in area planted.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture last month projected planted area at 9.97 million acres, down 15 percent from the previous year.
Ohio and Indiana's area fell a collective 300,000 acres to 1.25 million and 700,000 respectively. The acreage in Illinois fell more sharply to 1.15 million from 1.65 million.
